content.fetal_development: In week one there is no embryo yet; this week is counted from the first day of your last period. Your body is preparing for ovulation and possible implantation.
content.mother_body_changes: Your body is shedding the previous uterine lining and preparing a new cycle. You may notice typical period symptoms; no pregnancy signs yet.
content.dos_and_donts: Start a daily folic acid supplement now and avoid alcohol and smoking. Eat a balanced diet, sleep well, and check any medication with your doctor.
content.care_plan: If planning pregnancy, this is a good week to begin folic acid and track your period date. A pre-conception checkup can help.
content.body_adaptation: Your body is still in its normal state and pregnancy adaptation has not begun. Focus on physical and mental readiness.
content.emotional_status: You may feel a mix of excitement and worry about the journey ahead. Staying calm and realistic helps; talking with your partner can reassure you.
content.key_nutrition: Include 400 mcg folic acid daily, leafy greens and whole grains. Drink enough water and limit caffeine.
content.physical_activity: Keep up light activity like walking and gentle stretching to prepare your body. Avoid very intense exercise without advice.
content.tests_and_checkups: A pre-conception visit to review general health and vaccinations is helpful. No pregnancy-specific test is needed this week.

faq.question: Why is week one counted without an embryo?
faq.answer: Gestational age is measured from the first day of your last period, so the first two weeks come before conception.

faq.question: When should I start folic acid?
faq.answer: It is best to begin folic acid even before conception to support healthy neural development.

content.fetal_development: At week twenty, the halfway point, the fetus is about the size of a banana, roughly 25 cm crown-to-heel and nearly 300 g. The baby moves regularly, swallows, and has sleep-wake patterns, while hair and nails grow.
content.mother_body_changes: The bump is now clearly visible and baby movements are felt regularly. You may have heartburn, mild shortness of breath or leg swelling, and stretch marks can appear.
content.dos_and_donts: Continue healthy eating and supplements and sleep on your side, preferably the left. Avoid heavy meals to reduce heartburn and stay active.
content.care_plan: Week twenty is the usual time for the anomaly scan; if not done, arrange it. Keep regular visits and blood-pressure checks and begin noting fetal movements.
content.body_adaptation: The uterus reaches the navel and the body has adjusted to a new center of gravity. Pressure on the stomach can cause heartburn as circulation works strongly.
content.emotional_status: Reaching the halfway point often brings a sense of achievement and hope. The bond deepens through the baby’s movements; keep up self-care and rest.
content.key_nutrition: Continue iron, calcium and protein and eat small frequent meals for heartburn. Avoid spicy and greasy foods and get enough water and fiber.
content.physical_activity: Walking, swimming and prenatal yoga are ideal this week. Pelvic floor exercises help prepare for birth; avoid long back-lying.
content.tests_and_checkups: The anomaly scan is usually done in weeks 18 to 22, often this week, examining the baby’s full anatomy. Routine visits include blood pressure, weight and fetal heartbeat.

faq.question: Why is the week-20 scan important?
faq.answer: It reviews the baby’s full anatomy and detects many structural anomalies at this stage.

faq.question: What helps heartburn?
faq.answer: Small meals, avoiding spicy and greasy food, and not lying down right after eating help; see a doctor if severe.

content.fetal_development: At week forty, the due date, the fetus is about the size of a small pumpkin, roughly 51.2 cm and nearly 3.4 kg. The baby is fully grown and ready to be born, with skull bones still soft to pass through the birth canal.
content.mother_body_changes: You may have strong pelvic pressure, contractions and restlessness. Labor signs like the bloody show or waters breaking may appear, and waiting can be tiring.
content.dos_and_donts: Continue healthy eating and supplements and take labor signs seriously. Go to the hospital at once if your waters break, you bleed, or contractions are regular; keep counting movements.
content.care_plan: Visits continue and the doctor monitors the baby and cervix. If labor doesn’t start a few days past the due date, the doctor may consider induction; be ready to go in.
content.body_adaptation: The cervix opens and readies for birth and contractions may begin any moment. The body brings all its readiness to labor in this final stage of the pregnancy journey.
content.emotional_status: You may feel a mix of intense excitement, impatience and birth anxiety. If you go past due you may feel a little discouraged, which is normal; keep calm and supported.
content.key_nutrition: Continue iron, calcium, protein and fiber and drink enough water. Light, energizing foods help for labor, and small meals digest more easily.
content.physical_activity: Light walking may help start or progress labor. Practice breathing exercises to manage pain, listen to your body, and rest enough.
content.tests_and_checkups: Visits include blood pressure, weight, a cervical check and fetal heartbeat monitoring. Past due, the doctor may advise an ultrasound and a non-stress test (NST) for reassurance.

faq.question: What if I go past my due date?
faq.answer: Up to week 42 can be normal; the doctor monitors the baby’s health and induces labor if needed.

faq.question: What is labor induction?
faq.answer: It is a medical way to start labor, done by the doctor when you are past due or for medical reasons.
